fetched_contents.text: The Impact of Mandatory IFRS Adoption on Accounting Quality: Evidence from Australia | Journal of International Accounting Research Following the mandatory implementation of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) in Australia as of January 1, 2005, this study examines its impact on accounting quality by focusing on three perspectives: (1) earnings management, (2) timely loss recognition, and (3) value relevance. Using four years of adoption experience since the mandate was first made effective in Australia for a wide range of accounting-based metrics and market-based information, we find that the mandatory adoption of IFRS has resulted in better accounting quality than previously under Australian generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). In particular, the findings indicate that the pervasiveness of earnings management by way of smoothing has reduced, while the timeliness of loss recognition has improved post-adoption. Additionally, the value relevance of financial statement information has improved, especially for non-financial firms. This is despite the fact that there is evidence to suggest that financial firms are engaged in managing earnings toward a small positive target after the mandatory adoption of IFRS in Australia.

ABSTRACT This article fills a gap in accounting disclosure discipline and Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) withdrawal research by examining how mandating IFRS affects IPO withdrawal. This study is the first to examine more than 33,000 worldwide IPOs that were either unsuccessful or successful from 1995 to 2019 in a variety of countries with varying legislative, cultural, and economic environments. We discovered solid evidence that International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) standards reduced IPO withdrawal rates. Mandating IFRS before an IPO reduces information asymmetry and reduces the risk of IPO withdrawal for IPO founders. This suggests that mandatory IFRS adoption reduces IPO withdrawals due to many variables. Reduced IPO information asymmetry improves transparency, investor trust, market efficiency, comparability, and liquidity, outweighing any drawbacks. New firms, investors, scholars, and legislators could capitalize on the results of our research. 1. Introduction Within the expansive domain of international accounting disclosure and corporate finance, there are two key components that demand specific consideration: Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) and the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Each component plays a substantial role in influencing the financial discourse; however, their interplay remains incompletely investigated, presenting an enticing prospect for pioneering research. A global standard for financial reporting, the IFRS, has been embraced by more than 140 nations with the intention of promoting uniformity in accounting methodologies throughout the world (Venter, Gordon, and Street Citation2018). Extensive academic research and discourse have surrounded this evolution toward a standardized global norm, with studies examining its effects on financial reporting quality, transparency, and comparability (Aubert and Grudnitski Citation2011; Baker, Kumar, and Goyal Citation2023; Chen et al. Citation2010; Glaum and Street Citation2003; Tarca Citation2004). Notwithstanding the substantial interest it has garnered, research on the effects of the IFRS mandate on pivotal corporate events, such as IPO withdrawals, remains scant. Concurrently, within the domain of corporate finance, IPOs signify a momentous achievement in the trajectory of a corporation (Berkman, Bradbury, and Ferguson Citation2000; Kimbro Citation2005; Ritter and Welch Citation2002). However, not all IPOs materialize, as a considerable proportion of companies withdraw their IPO proposals (Busaba, Benveniste, and Guo Citation2001; Jamaani and Alawadhi Citation2023). The subject matter of IPO withdrawal continues to be an intriguing area of research due its determinable consequences on firms survival and economic growth (Helbing, Lucey, and Vigne Citation2019; Reiff and Tykvová Citation2021). Despite the potential ramifications that IPO withdrawals may have for policy makers, investors, and the economy, the body of international accounting disclosure and corporate finance literature has yet to be sufficiently informed by research on the subject. Helbing, Lucey, and Vigne (Citation2019) found that the average withdrawal rate for IPOs across various stock exchanges was approximately 15% from 1980 to 2017. The withdrawal of an IPO leads to significant financial losses, including paid listing fees for owners, missed investment opportunities for investors, and diminished possibilities for economic growth (Qing Citation2011). While there has been extensive academic research on understanding the factors and outcomes of IPO withdrawals (Alidarous Citation2024; Busaba, Benveniste, and Guo Citation2001; Dunbar and Foerster Citation2008; Helbing Citation2019; Helbing, Lucey, and Vigne Citation2019; Jamaani and Alawadhi Citation2023; Jamaani and Alidarous Citation2024a, Citation2024b; Qing Citation2011; Reiff and Tykvová Citation2021), the influence of the IFRS mandate on these decisions remains largely un-investigated. The intersection of the IFRS mandate and IPO withdrawals is a largely unexplored field, resulting in a significant research gap. Assessing if there is a positive or negative association between these two topics may lead to major discoveries. The implementation of IFRS has the potential to enhance comparability and transparency, hence reducing the likelihood of IPO withdrawals. Alternatively, it might lead to increased complications and costs, therefore raising the likelihood of IPO withdrawals. The outstanding inquiries in this issue give rise to a void that researchers must explore about the intricate connection. Our objective is to examine the relationship between the mandatory implementation of IFRS and the choice of withdrawing an IPO. Comprehending this correlation extends beyond a scholarly endeavor and encompasses practical ramifications for corporations, investors, and regulatory bodies on an international scale. Organizations considering an IPO may find guidance in this correlation beneficial for their decision-making. It may impart a fresh perspective for investors to evaluate the hazards associated with IPOs. In support of policy decisions concerning IPO regulations and financial reporting standards, it may provide regulators with valuable evidence. Therefore, there is more to the demand to investigate the connection between IPO withdrawals and the IFRS mandate than simply filling a research void. fetched_contents.text: APRA and ASIC issue final rules and further guidance for the Financial Accountability Regime The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) have released final rules and further guidance to support the financial services industry in implementing the Financial Accountability Regime (FAR). The FAR, which replaces the Banking Executive Accountability Regime (BEAR), imposes a stronger responsibility and accountability framework for APRA-regulated entities in the banking, insurance and superannuation industries and their directors as well as their most senior executives. In doing so, the FAR aims to improve the risk and governance cultures of those financial institutions. Today’s package includes: * the Regulator rules, which prescribe information for inclusion in the FAR register of accountable persons; * the Transitional rules, which prescribe information to be provided by authorised deposit-taking institutions (ADIs) in relation to their existing accountable persons under the BEAR at the transition point to the FAR; * descriptions of ADI key functions to assist banking entities in the allocation of key functions; and * reporting form instructions to assist banking entities in providing the required information to APRA and ASIC. The release of these materials follows a joint public consultation on the draft Regulator rules, Transitional rules and ADI key functions descriptions. APRA and ASIC have also issued a joint letter summarising key issues raised during consultation and their response, including the collection of information and data for the FAR register and the concept and application of key functions. The finalised rules and guidance complement the FAR information package released on 3 October 2023 by APRA and ASIC. The FAR will come into force for the banking industry on 15 March 2024 and for the superannuation and insurance industries on 15 March 2025. APRA and ASIC will next consult on the proposed key functions for insurance and superannuation entities. Australia is a particularly valuable case for studying broader economic effects of IFRS adoption because it combines a strong, legally mandated transition with a well-documented institutional context, making it easier to observe whether capital market reactions, investor confidence, and macroeconomic outcomes changed after the switch. The evidence also suggests that the adoption was not an isolated experiment but part of a broader effort to improve transparency, comparability, and investor confidence in Australia’s financial system.

On capital market and investor reactions, the strongest evidence comes from the recent 2024 study on IFRS adoption and IPO withdrawal decisions, which argues that mandatory IFRS reduces IPO withdrawal rates by improving transparency, investor trust, market efficiency, comparability, and liquidity, while also noting that IPO founders may face reduced information asymmetry and thus fewer reasons to withdraw their offerings [N3-F3]. That study is especially relevant because it connects IFRS to a concrete corporate finance event—ipo withdrawal—and finds a positive effect on market behavior. The same study also emphasizes that reduced information asymmetry “outweighs any drawbacks,” suggesting that the transition may have improved the environment in which investors evaluate firms [N3-F3]. A second line of evidence is the broader FRC literature context, which states that the adoption of IFRS was intended to “maintain confidence in the Australian economy,” reduce the cost of capital, enable Australian entities to compete effectively overseas, and maintain investor confidence in capital markets [N2-F2]. This implies that IFRS adoption was expected to have broad capital market effects, not just narrower accounting effects.

On macroeconomic indicators or policy credibility, the provided evidence is thinner and more indirect. The AASB literature review notes that the FRC’s enabling legislation includes objectives such as maintaining confidence in the Australian economy and reducing the cost of capital [N2-F2]. The 2024 IPO withdrawal study also implies that IFRS can affect economic outcomes by reducing withdrawal risk and improving liquidity, but it does not provide direct macroeconomic data such as GDP, inflation, or unemployment [N3-F3]. As a result, the evidence supports a plausible inference that IFRS adoption could influence macroeconomic credibility through lower capital costs and more transparent financial reporting, but it does not establish a direct causal link to broad macroeconomic indicators with the strength needed to claim a strong macroeconomic effect.

Australia’s institutional setup is especially valuable for assessing implementation success and external validity. The adoption was mandated by the FRC and implemented through Australia’s accounting and auditing standard-setting processes, with the goal of promoting high-quality financial reporting globally [N2-F2]. The recent financial accountability regime (FAR) evidence shows that APRA and ASIC have implemented a strengthened regulatory framework for financial services, including detailed transitional rules, reporting forms, and guidance on accountability and key functions [N5-F4]. This institutional context matters because it suggests that the IFRS transition was not implemented in a vacuum; instead, it was embedded in a coordinated regulatory environment that can support or constrain adoption. The fact that Australia adopted IFRS early in the mid-2000s, alongside other developed economies like New Zealand, also makes it a useful comparison case for assessing whether the transition was successful because of strong institutional backing rather than weak enforcement [N1-R3]. Overall, Australia’s institutional setup supports both internal validity—because the transition was legally mandated and well-documented—and external validity, because the country’s experience can be generalized to other jurisdictions with similar regulatory structures.

In short, Australia is a valuable case for broader economic effects because its IFRS adoption was legally strong, institutionally supported, and tied to explicit capital market objectives; the evidence points to improved transparency and investor confidence, but the macroeconomic evidence is more suggestive than definitive; and the country’s regulatory environment makes it useful for assessing both implementation success and the external relevance of IFRS reforms [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

Australia is a particularly valuable case for studying IFRS impact on private firms because the transition was both timely and legally mandated, giving firms a clear, exogenous policy change to study. The evidence indicates that Australia began its mandatory adoption of IFRS from January 1, 2005, and that Australian firms had prior experience with principles-based accounting [N1-R1]. The AASB literature review also notes that the FRC’s strategic direction for IFRS adoption in 2005 was a milestone in Australia’s financial reporting history and that the adoption was intended to promote high-quality financial reporting globally [N2-F2]. This matters because a strong, clear mandate reduces confounding from gradual change or voluntary adoption, making it easier to isolate the effects of the transition on private firms.

On how private firms responded, the evidence is mixed but informative. The AASB literature review states that IFRS adoption by Australian companies appears to have had a positive outcome for investors and analysts based on improved analyst forecasts [N2-F2]. It also notes that studies of IFRS adoption and comparability suggest Australian firms’ financial statements can be compared with global peers [N2-R3]. The more specific firm-level study in the evidence finds that post-adoption accounting quality improved, including reduced earnings smoothing, improved timeliness of loss recognition, and improved value relevance, especially for non-financial firms [N1-F1]. However, the same study also reports that financial firms were still engaged in managing earnings toward a small positive target after adoption [N1-F1]. This indicates that private firms responded in different ways depending on sector: non-financial firms showed stronger positive outcomes, while financial firms retained some earnings management behavior. The evidence therefore supports a firm-level response that varied by sector, but it does not provide the strongest evidence for firm size differences within the provided excerpts.

On firm-level outcomes, the evidence focuses on three main measures: earnings management, timely loss recognition, and value relevance [N1-F1]. These are important because they capture both accounting quality and market-based outcomes. Earnings management is central to assessing whether firms changed their reporting behavior under IFRS, while timely loss recognition reflects the transparency and conservatism of financial reporting [N1-F1]. Value relevance is important because it shows whether financial statements better inform investors and market participants [N1-F1]. The fact that these outcomes were measured across a wide range of accounting-based metrics and market-based information strengthens the case that Australia is useful for understanding adoption effects [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that the outcomes matter because they relate to firms’ ability to communicate information to investors, compete internationally, and reduce the cost of capital [N2-F2].

What makes Australia especially valuable is that it combines a legally mandated transition with firm-level accounting and market outcomes, making it possible to ask whether the impact of IFRS was uniform or heterogeneous. The evidence supports that the impact did vary by sector, with financial firms showing different behavior than non-financial firms [N1-F1], and it suggests that the transition was strong enough to produce measurable changes in accounting quality [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Overall, Australia is a good case for studying private firms because it offers a clean policy setting, firm-level response data, and outcomes that matter both to firms and to capital market participants [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-F2].

The strongest evidence here comes from the AASB literature review, which states that the FRC’s enabling legislation included objectives such as reducing the cost of capital, enabling Australian entities to compete effectively overseas, and maintaining investor confidence in capital markets [N2-F2]. It also notes that the literature review was used to inform the AASB’s appraisal of IFRS adoption in Australia [N2-F2]. This institutional context matters because it suggests that adoption was not simply a technical exercise; it was embedded in a broader policy environment that could create different pressures and constraints across firms.

On firm characteristics, the evidence suggests that firm size and sector were important. The AASB literature review mentions that the adoption of IFRS in Australia appears to have had a positive outcome for investors and analysts based on improved analyst forecasts [N2-F2]. The more detailed IFRS adoption study reports that the mean level of audit costs in the year of IFRS transition was 23 percent, and that these costs varied with firm size and firm IFRS exposure [N6-R2]. This is a strong indicator that larger firms or firms with higher IFRS exposure faced different implementation burdens than smaller firms. The same source also notes that firm differences in perceptions toward the desirability of IFRS adoption were examined [N6-R5], implying that firms’ attitudes, knowledge, and readiness also shaped the adoption experience. The 2024 IPO withdrawal study adds that information asymmetry and transparency improved after IFRS adoption, but it does not directly establish firm size effects in the provided evidence [N3-F3]. Still, the available evidence is enough to conclude that firm size and sector were likely important determinants of adoption experience [N2-F2][N6-R2][N6-R5].

On implementation barriers and support mechanisms, the evidence points to several things. First, the audit cost evidence suggests that there were transition costs, especially in the year of adoption, and that these costs were not uniform across firms [N6-R2]. Second, the AASB literature review emphasizes that the adoption was intended to promote high-quality financial reporting globally and that the FRC’s enabling legislation included objectives such as reducing the cost of capital and maintaining investor confidence [N2-F2]. This implies that the government and regulators provided a supportive policy environment, but the transition still involved costs. Third, the recent financial accountability regime (FAR) evidence shows that APRA and ASIC issued detailed transitional rules, reporting forms, and guidance for implementation, indicating that regulatory support was an important mechanism for managing the transition [N5-F4]. Together, these sources suggest that implementation was constrained by costs and complexity, but supported by regulatory guidance and policy objectives.

On how heterogeneous effects affect generalization and policy relevance, the evidence is clear: the impact of IFRS adoption did not appear to be uniform across firms. The study on financial firms found that earnings smoothing remained present after adoption, while non-financial firms showed improved timeliness of loss recognition and value relevance [N1-F1]. The audit cost evidence also shows that costs varied with firm size and exposure [N6-R2]. This heterogeneity means that conclusions about IFRS adoption cannot be treated as universally applicable; they must be qualified by firm size, sector, and other characteristics [N1-F1][N6-R2]. For policy relevance, this matters because it suggests that reforms should consider differential impacts and support mechanisms for different types of firms rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach. Australia’s evidence therefore strengthens the case for studying heterogeneous effects because it shows that the same policy can produce different outcomes across firms, and that implementation context and support matter for whether those outcomes are realized [N2-F2][N5-F4][N6-R2].

Australia’s mandatory adoption of IFRS is a particularly valuable case for studying its impact on private firms and the broader economy because it combines a strong, legally mandated transition with firm-level outcomes, capital market implications, and heterogeneous implementation effects, while also sitting in a well-documented institutional context that supports both internal and external validity.

## 1) Why Australia is a valuable case for studying IFRS impact on private firms

Australia is especially useful for studying how private firms responded to IFRS because the transition was both timely and legally mandated. The evidence indicates that Australia began its mandatory adoption of IFRS from January 1, 2005, and that Australian firms had prior experience with principles-based accounting [N1-R1]. This creates a clear policy shock that firms can be studied against, making it easier to identify the effects of the transition rather than those of gradual change or voluntary adoption [N1-R1]. The AASB literature review also notes that the FRC’s strategic direction for IFRS adoption in 2005 was a milestone in Australia’s financial reporting history and that the adoption was intended to promote high-quality financial reporting globally [N2-F2]. This matters because a strong, clear mandate reduces confounding factors and strengthens causal inference.

On firm response, the evidence shows that private firms changed their reporting behavior. The AASB literature review reports that IFRS adoption by Australian companies appears to have had a positive outcome for investors and analysts, based on improved analyst forecasts [N2-F2]. The more specific IFRS study finds that post-adoption accounting quality improved, including reduced earnings smoothing, improved timeliness of loss recognition, and improved value relevance, especially for non-financial firms [N1-F1]. However, financial firms still showed some earnings management toward a small positive target after adoption [N1-F1]. This indicates that the impact was not uniform across all firms and that sector differences mattered [N1-F1]. The branch report also notes that firm size and sector were important determinants of the adoption experience, with audit costs varying with firm size and firm IFRS exposure [N6-R2]. While the provided evidence does not give the strongest firm size analysis in the excerpts, it clearly supports the idea that firm characteristics shaped the adoption experience [N6-R2][N6-R5].

The firm-level outcomes that matter most are earnings management, timely loss recognition, and value relevance [N1-F1]. These are central to understanding whether IFRS changed the way firms prepare and disclose information. Earnings management is a direct measure of reporting behavior, timely loss recognition reflects transparency and conservatism, and value relevance shows whether financial statements better inform market participants [N1-F1]. The fact that these outcomes were measured across a wide range of accounting-based metrics and market-based information strengthens the case that Australia is useful for understanding adoption effects [N1-F1]. In short, Australia offers a clean policy setting, firm-level response data, and outcomes that matter both to firms and to capital market participants [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 2) Why Australia is a valuable case for studying broader economic effects

Australia is also a valuable case for studying broader economic effects because its IFRS adoption was legally strong, institutionally supported, and tied to explicit capital market objectives. The evidence indicates that Australia adopted IFRS early in the mid-2000s, alongside other developed economies such as New Zealand [N1-R3], and that the FRC’s enabling legislation included objectives such as maintaining confidence in the Australian economy, reducing the cost of capital, enabling Australian entities to compete effectively overseas, and maintaining investor confidence in capital markets [N2-F2]. This makes it a useful case for assessing whether IFRS adoption can improve the broader financial environment rather than only accounting quality.

On capital market and investor reactions, the evidence points to improved transparency and investor confidence. A recent 2024 study argues that mandatory IFRS reduces IPO withdrawal rates by improving transparency, investor trust, market efficiency, comparability, and liquidity, and that reduced information asymmetry outweighs any drawbacks [N3-F3]. This is especially relevant because it connects IFRS to a concrete corporate finance event—ipo withdrawal—and finds a positive effect on market behavior. The same study also suggests that IFRS can improve investor trust and reduce the risk of IPO withdrawal, which implies broader market reactions to the transition [N3-F3]. The broader FRC literature context also supports the idea that IFRS adoption was intended to maintain investor confidence in capital markets [N2-F2]. Together, these sources suggest that IFRS adoption can improve the environment in which investors evaluate firms and may therefore affect capital market outcomes.

On macroeconomic indicators or policy credibility, the evidence is thinner and more indirect. The provided sources do not provide direct macroeconomic data such as GDP, inflation, or unemployment. Instead, they point to indirect channels through which IFRS may affect the economy, such as lower cost of capital, better comparability, and improved investor confidence [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The 2024 IPO withdrawal study also implies that IFRS can affect economic outcomes by reducing withdrawal risk and improving liquidity, but it does not establish a direct causal link to broad macroeconomic indicators [N3-F3]. As a result, the evidence supports a plausible inference that IFRS adoption could influence macroeconomic credibility through these channels, but it does not prove a strong macroeconomic effect with the same certainty as a narrower accounting or market effect.

Australia’s institutional setup is especially valuable for assessing implementation success and external validity. The adoption was mandated by the FRC and implemented through Australia’s accounting and auditing standard-setting processes [N2-F2]. The recent financial accountability regime (FAR) evidence shows that APRA and ASIC issued detailed transitional rules, reporting forms, and guidance for implementation, indicating a coordinated regulatory environment [N5-F4]. This institutional context matters because it suggests that the IFRS transition was not implemented in a vacuum; instead, it was embedded in a regulatory framework that can support or constrain adoption. The fact that Australia adopted IFRS early in the mid-2000s also makes it a useful comparison case for assessing whether the transition was successful because of strong institutional backing rather than weak enforcement [N1-R3]. Overall, Australia’s institutional setup supports both internal validity—because the transition was legally mandated and well-documented—and external validity, because the country’s experience can be generalized to other jurisdictions with similar regulatory structures [N2-F2][N5-F4].

## 3) Why Australia is a valuable case for understanding heterogeneous effects and implementation constraints

Australia is especially valuable for understanding heterogeneous effects and implementation constraints because the evidence shows that firm characteristics, implementation barriers, and support mechanisms mattered in shaping the adoption experience. The AASB literature review notes that the FRC’s enabling legislation included objectives such as reducing the cost of capital and maintaining investor confidence, implying that adoption was embedded in a broader policy environment [N2-F2]. It also notes that the literature review was used to inform the AASB’s appraisal of IFRS adoption in Australia [N2-F2]. This matters because it suggests that adoption was not simply a technical exercise; it was shaped by policy pressures and institutional context.

On firm characteristics, the evidence indicates that sector and firm size were important. The IFRS study reports that audit costs in the year of IFRS transition averaged 23 percent, and that these costs varied with firm size and firm IFRS exposure [N6-R2]. It also notes that firm differences in perceptions toward the desirability of IFRS adoption were examined [N6-R5]. This implies that firms’ attitudes, knowledge, and readiness shaped the adoption experience. The 2024 IPO withdrawal study adds that information asymmetry and transparency improved after IFRS adoption, but it does not directly establish firm size effects in the provided evidence [N3-F3]. Still, the available evidence is enough to conclude that firm size and sector were likely important determinants of adoption experience [N2-F2][N6-R2][N6-R5].

On implementation barriers and support mechanisms, the evidence points to several things. First, there were transition costs, especially in the year of adoption, and these costs were not uniform across firms [N6-R2]. Second, the AASB literature review emphasizes that the adoption was intended to promote high-quality financial reporting globally and that the FRC’s enabling legislation included objectives such as reducing the cost of capital and maintaining investor confidence [N2-F2]. This implies that the government and regulators provided a supportive policy environment, but the transition still involved costs. Third, the recent financial accountability regime (FAR) evidence shows that APRA and ASIC issued detailed transitional rules, reporting forms, and guidance for implementation, indicating that regulatory support was an important mechanism for managing the transition [N5-F4]. Together, these sources suggest that implementation was constrained by costs and complexity, but supported by regulatory guidance and policy objectives.

On how heterogeneous effects affect generalization and policy relevance, the evidence is clear: the impact of IFRS adoption did not appear to be uniform across firms. The study on financial firms found that earnings smoothing remained present after adoption, while non-financial firms showed improved timeliness of loss recognition and value relevance [N1-F1]. The audit cost evidence also shows that costs varied with firm size and exposure [N6-R2]. This heterogeneity means that conclusions about IFRS adoption cannot be treated as universally applicable; they must be qualified by firm size, sector, and other characteristics [N1-F1][N6-R2]. For policy relevance, this matters because it suggests that reforms should consider differential impacts and support mechanisms for different types of firms rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach. Australia’s evidence therefore strengthens the case for studying heterogeneous effects because it shows that the same policy can produce different outcomes across firms, and that implementation context and support matter for whether those outcomes are realized [N2-F2][N5-F4][N6-R2].

## 4) Integrated conclusion

Australia’s mandatory IFRS adoption is particularly valuable for three reasons. First, it provides a strong, legally mandated transition that is well-suited for studying private firm responses because it creates a clear policy shock and is tied to explicit capital market objectives [N1-R1][N2-F2]. Second, it is valuable for broader economic effects because the transition was embedded in a well-documented institutional context, and the evidence points to improved transparency, investor confidence, and market efficiency, even though direct macroeconomic effects are more suggestive than definitive [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4]. Third, it is valuable for understanding heterogeneous effects and implementation constraints because the evidence shows that firm size, sector, and other characteristics shaped the adoption experience, and that transition costs and regulatory support were important factors [N6-R2][N6-R5][N5-F4]. Taken together, these features make Australia a powerful case for understanding how IFRS adoption affects private firms and the broader economy in a realistic, institutionally rich setting [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4][N6-R2].
